_comment: Pan-African colonial-acquisition knowledge base for bm_adjudicate.py. Scope: the whole of Africa. The shortlister advances any record whose provenance text matches an alias here (high recall by design); Haiku then weighs the matched flags against mitigating features and must quote the record. Aliases include object-type priors (a Benin brass plaque, an Ethiopian tabot, a Great Zimbabwe soapstone bird) so the object's identity alone can shortlist it regardless of acquisition date. Names are stored 'Surname, Forename' where possible to match BM's convention. Expand freely. | Patched with the pan-African registry (africa_redflags/, sources in SOURCES.md): every added entry is a documented suspicion signal for review, not proof.

incidents.name: Benin Punitive Expedition (1897)
incidents.summary: British force sacked Benin City in Feb 1897; thousands of brass plaques and ivories were seized and dispersed.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1897-1905; Benin City; donor Foreign Office or a participating officer; brass/ivory court object.

incidents.name: Capture of Maqdala / Magdala (1868)
incidents.summary: British expedition stormed Emperor Tewodros II's fortress at Maqdala in 1868; tabots, crosses, crowns and manuscripts were carried off and auctioned.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1868-1872; Maqdala/Abyssinia; tabot/cross/crown/manuscript; donor an expedition participant or R.R. Holmes.

incidents.name: Anglo-Asante Wars / sacks of Kumasi (1874, 1896, 1900)
incidents.summary: British forces sacked Kumasi in 1874, occupied it in 1896 (exiling Asantehene Prempeh), and again in 1900; gold regalia and palace contents were seized.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1874-1901; Kumasi/Manhyia Palace; donor Gold Coast Government or an officer; gold regalia.

incidents.name: Franco-Dahomean War / sack of Abomey (1892)
incidents.summary: French forces under Dodds took Abomey in 1892; royal thrones, bocio figures and regalia were seized.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1892-1900; Abomey/Dahomey; royal regalia/throne/bocio.

incidents.name: Reconquest of Sudan / Omdurman and Khartoum (1885, 1898)
incidents.summary: Fall of Khartoum (1885) and the Anglo-Egyptian defeat of the Mahdist state at Omdurman (1898); banners, arms and relics were taken.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1885-1901; Mahdist jibba/banner/arms; donor a participating officer (e.g. Kitchener).

incidents.name: Anglo-Zulu War (1879)
incidents.summary: British invasion of the Zulu Kingdom; after Ulundi the royal kraal was burned and regalia, weapons and the king's effects were taken.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1879-1884; Zululand/Ulundi; royal regalia, isicholo, iklwa/assegai, donor a soldier.

incidents.name: Matabele Wars / occupation of Bulawayo (1893-1896)
incidents.summary: British South Africa Company forces occupied Bulawayo and overthrew King Lobengula; royal and ritual objects were seized. Great Zimbabwe soapstone birds were removed 1889-1906.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1893-1906; Matabeleland/Rhodesia/Bulawayo; via the BSA Company; Great Zimbabwe soapstone bird.

incidents.name: Removal of Great Zimbabwe antiquities (1889-1906)
incidents.summary: Soapstone birds and other objects were removed from the Great Zimbabwe ruins by BSA Company men, Cecil Rhodes and antiquarians.
incidents.museum_signals: Soapstone bird; Great Zimbabwe/Mashonaland findspot; BSA Company or Rhodes provenance.

incidents.name: Conquest of the Sokoto Caliphate (1897-1903)
incidents.summary: Lugard's campaigns took Bida (1897), Kano and Sokoto (1903); palace libraries, manuscripts, arms and regalia were seized.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1897-1906; Sokoto/Kano/Bida/Nupe; Arabic manuscript, arms; via Northern Nigeria administration or Lugard.

incidents.name: Anglo-Aro War (1901-1902)
incidents.summary: British expedition destroyed the Aro Confederacy and the Long Juju oracle; Igbo ritual objects were removed.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1901-1906; Arochukwu/southeastern Nigeria; Igbo ritual object.

incidents.name: Herero and Nama genocide (1904-1908, German South-West Africa)
incidents.summary: German colonial forces committed genocide against the Herero and Nama; human remains (skulls) and cultural objects were taken for 'racial science' and as trophies.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1904-1915; German South-West Africa/Namibia; human/ancestral remains; Witbooi objects.

incidents.name: French conquest of Madagascar (1895)
incidents.summary: French forces took Antananarivo in 1895 and abolished the Merina monarchy; royal collections from the Rova were dispersed.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1895-1905; Antananarivo/Merina; royal regalia/relic.

incidents.name: French conquest of the Tukulor Empire / fall of Segou (1890)
incidents.summary: French forces under Archinard took Segou in 1890; the library and treasury of the Tukulor Empire (El Hadj Umar Tall's state) were seized.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1890-1900; Segou/French Sudan/Mali; Arabic manuscript, regalia.

incidents.name: Fall of the Wassoulou Empire / capture of Samori Ture (1898)
incidents.summary: French forces defeated Samori Ture's Wassoulou Empire (Guinea/Mali/Ivory Coast); regalia and arms were taken.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1892-1902; Wassoulou/upper Niger; regalia, arms.

incidents.name: Portuguese conquest of the Gaza Empire / Gungunhana (1895)
incidents.summary: Portuguese forces captured King Gungunhana in 1895 and dismantled the Gaza Empire; royal objects were removed.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1895-1905; southern Mozambique/Gaza; royal regalia.

incidents.name: Conquest of Bunyoro and East African campaigns (1890s-1900s)
incidents.summary: British campaigns against Bunyoro (Kabalega), the Nandi and coastal Mazrui; royal and ritual objects were seized, often via the IBEA Company and colonial officers.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1890-1910; Uganda/Kenya; royal regalia; via IBEA Company or a district officer.

incidents.name: Congo Free State / coercive collecting (1885-1908)
incidents.summary: Under Leopold II's Congo Free State, ethnographic objects (power figures, Kuba royal art) were collected under extreme coercion and violence.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1885-1920; Congo/Kongo/Kuba/Luba; nkisi/minkisi/ndop; via a Congo company or agent.

incidents.name: German Cameroon / Bamum and Duala (1884-1914)
incidents.summary: In German Kamerun, Bamum royal beadwork and thrones and Duala objects entered German collections under colonial pressure.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1884-1918; Cameroon/Bamum/Foumban; beaded throne/regalia; German colonial provenance.

incidents.name: Italian occupation of Ethiopia (1935-1941)
incidents.summary: Italian forces looted Ethiopian treasures including the Aksum obelisk and the Lion of Judah statue.
incidents.museum_signals: Acquired 1935-1945; Ethiopia/Aksum/Addis Ababa; imperial regalia.

incidents.name: Removal of Egyptian and Nubian antiquities (excavation / partage)
incidents.summary: Egyptian and Nubian antiquities left the country via excavation, the partage system, and outright removal under colonial administration. Contested but distinct from military looting; weigh mitigating documentation carefully.
incidents.museum_signals: Egyptian/Nubian antiquity; excavated/exported pre-1930; human remains raise a separate repatriation concern.

actors.name: Curt von Pavel
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that he led the 1902 punitive expedition that looted the Ngonnso deity and other treasures from the Nso Palace before burning it, then donated Ngonnso in 1903 to the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation claiming it was a gift from the absent Fon. Objects with a von Pavel donor line warrant provenance review. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: The Restitution Journey of Ngonnso — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/the-restitution-journey-of-ngonnso-from-the-nso-kingdom-in-cameroon/]

actors.name: Max Buchner
actors.role: German colonial officer; interim imperial representative in Kamerun 1884-85; later first director, Munich ethnographic museum
actors.why_flag: ORA and mapping.postkolonial document that he seized the sacred Tangué (ship prow) of King Kum'a Mbape (Lock Priso) during the December 1884 German bombardment and burning of the Douala palace, described the plunder in his memoirs, and gave it in 1885 to the Royal Ethnographic Collection Munich (now Museum Fünf Kontinente); subject of a pending restitution claim. Cameroonian material with his donor line is a review signal. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: The Tangué — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/the-tangue-belonging-of-the-bele-bele-family-of-douala-kingdom/ ; Der Raub des Tangué — https://mapping.postkolonial.net/article/der-raub-des-tangue]

actors.name: P. Wassmansdorf
actors.role: Official, colonial department of the German Foreign Office; donor to Linden-Museum
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that by 1902 he was in possession of Gaob Hendrik Witbooi's whip and Bible, looted during the 1893 Schutztruppe massacre at Hornkranz, and donated them to the Linden Museum, Stuttgart (returned to Namibia 2019). Namibian objects with this donor line warrant review; marker for Foreign Office channelling of war loot to museums. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Hendrik Witbooi Bible and Whip — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/hendrik-witbooi-gabemab-nanseb-bible-and-whip-repatriation-case/]

actors.name: Alfred Claud Hollis
actors.role: British colonial administrator, East Africa Protectorate
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that in 1908 he donated the sacred Ngadji drum — confiscated from the Pokomo community in 1902 — to the British Museum, where it remains in storage against the community's wishes. East African objects with a Hollis donor line are a review signal. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: The Return of Ngadji — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/the-return-of-ngadji-a-sacred-drum-stolen-from-the-pokomo-people/]

actors.name: Henry Christy
actors.role: British collector; founder of the Christy collection/fund (British Museum)
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that King Moshoeshoe's belongings, sent as a diplomatic gift for the 1862 London International Exposition, were afterwards sold to Christy, whose 1865 bequest carried them into the British Museum. CALIBRATION: the Christy bequest/fund is the BM's default ethnography acquisition channel and appears on enormous numbers of records — flag only in combination with episode/region/object-type signals, never on the name alone. Excluded from flat matching lists. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: 80 of King Moshoeshoe's Belongings — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/80-of-king-moshoeshoes-belongings/]

actors.name: Otto Kümmel
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that as Director General of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin he declined to release the looted Benin royal stools in 1936-38, approving only replicas at Oba Akenzua II's cost. His administration's retention decisions are a review signal for Benin material accessioned in Berlin. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Benin Royal Stools — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/the-restitution-efforts-of-oba-akenzua-ii-and-the-significance-of-the-benin-royal-stools/]

actors.name: Eckart von Sydow
actors.why_flag: ORA documents his 1936 role confirming the looted Benin royal stools in Luschan's catalogue during negotiations in which Berlin declined restitution — a documented participant in 1930s dealings around looted Benin objects. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Benin Royal Stools — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/the-restitution-efforts-of-oba-akenzua-ii-and-the-significance-of-the-benin-royal-stools/]

actors.name: Georg Steindorff
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that his 163-object collection was assembled 1903-1931 via purchases and excavations under the colonial-era partage de fouilles system, which Egypt contests. NOTE: Steindorff was himself later a victim of Nazi persecution; the flag concerns the partage channel, not personal wrongdoing. Likely out of scope for the BM Africa (ethnography) corpus — Egypt dept is catalogued separately. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: The Steindorff Case — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/selective-memory-and-the-steindorff-case-what-we-choose-to-forget/]

actors.name: Tom Zwiglaar
actors.why_flag: ORA documents him as the miner who removed the Kabwe Man skull from a disturbed burial context at Broken Hill Mine in June 1921, the first link in its transfer chain to London. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Kabwe Man — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/kabwe-man/]

actors.name: Ross Macartney
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that he transported the Kabwe Man skull to the British Museum in 1921 without the removal permit required under the 1912 Bushman Relics Proclamation, 'in effect making the acquisition and transfer to the British Museum illegal'. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Kabwe Man — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/kabwe-man/]

actors.name: Arthur Smith Woodward
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that he received and examined the Kabwe Man skull at the British Museum in 1921 (naming Homo rhodesiensis) — the receiving scientist in an acquisition effected without the legally required permit; flags early-20th-century BM intake of African remains for review. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Kabwe Man — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/kabwe-man/]

actors.name: Aleš Hrdlička
actors.why_flag: ORA documents the Smithsonian commissioned him c.1923-24 to report on 'The Rhodesian Man', confirming the dig disrupted an apparent burial site — a documented participant in racial-science-era study of removed African remains. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Kabwe Man — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/kabwe-man/]

actors.name: Jules Verreaux
actors.role: French naturalist, taxidermist and natural-history trader
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that from 1818 the Verreaux brothers were 'acquiring, stealing and trading natural history specimens from South Africa', including the 1830 theft of a freshly buried man's body, taxidermied and shipped to France ('El Negre de Banyoles'). Any Verreaux-sourced African human or natural-history material demands scrutiny. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Masalela — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/masalela-a-monna-wa-mosarwa-a-boetse-gae-the-remains-of-the-mosarwa-man-have-returned-home/]

actors.name: Édouard Verreaux
actors.role: French naturalist, taxidermist and natural-history trader
actors.why_flag: Named alongside his brother Jules in ORA's account of the 1818-1830 acquisition, theft and trading of Southern African natural-history specimens, including the grave-robbed body displayed as El Negre de Banyoles. Verreaux provenance is a standing review signal. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Masalela — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/masalela-a-monna-wa-mosarwa-a-boetse-gae-the-remains-of-the-mosarwa-man-have-returned-home/]

actors.name: Pieter Cezars
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that Sara Baartman was 'illegally sold to merchant Pieter Cezars and enslaved as a child' c.1797 — the first documented link in the chain of her exploitation and display in Europe. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: The Repatriation of Sara Baartman — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/3609/]

actors.name: Hendrik Cezar
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that he coerced Baartman to England in 1810 and exhibited her for profit; defendant in the 1810 Court of King's Bench case. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: The Repatriation of Sara Baartman — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/3609/]

actors.name: Alexander Dunlop
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that he conspired with the Cezar brothers to coerce Baartman from the Cape in 1810 under a 'dubious arrangement' and profited from her exhibition; defendant in the 1810 King's Bench case. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: The Repatriation of Sara Baartman — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/3609/]

actors.name: Georges Cuvier
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that after Baartman's death in 1816 he cast her body, removed her skeleton, brain and genitals, and preserved and displayed the remains at the Musée de l'Homme — retained until 2002. Cuvier-associated human material is a maximal review signal. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: The Repatriation of Sara Baartman — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/3609/]

actors.name: Erich Obst
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that, commissioned by the Geographische Gesellschaft in Hamburg, he led the expedition during which Isanzu ancestors' bones were removed from graves without community knowledge and sent to Hamburg 'as per the guidelines of racial sciences'. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Isanzu Community Perspectives — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/isanzu-community-perspectives-on-ancestral-human-remains-restitution-to-tanzania/]

actors.name: Neville Chittick
actors.role: British archaeologist; Conservator of Antiquities Tanganyika; first Director of BIEA
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that from 1957 he removed human remains from graves in Kilwa for research, then in 1961 moved them undocumented to the British Institute in Eastern Africa in Nairobi (returns only 2016-2023). Chittick-excavated material merits provenance and consent review. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Human Ancestors Return to Kilwa — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/human/]

actors.name: Pierre Harter
actors.role: French doctor and collector of Cameroonian sculpture
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that the Bamendou Tukah mask 'disappeared from the Bamendou palace' in 1957 and 'it was later found that Dr. Pierre Harter... had taken the mask, claiming he had been gifted numerous cultural belongings'; his 1991 bequest carried it into French national collections. Harter provenance on Grassfields material warrants gift-claim verification. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Bamendou Tukah Mask — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/bamendou-tukah-mask/]

actors.name: Eric von Rosen
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that during his 1911-12 expedition he collected the Batwa Lechwe Skin Cloaks and other 'rich and valuable belongings', donated to Sweden's National Museums of World Culture where they remain. Von Rosen-collected Zambian material is a review signal. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Lechwe Skin Cloaks of the Batwa — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/redressing-and-addressing-the-lechwe-skin-cloaks-of-the-batwa-people-1912-2025/]

actors.name: Ian Douglas Smith
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that in 1978-79 he 'incrementally and secretly deposited' what were in fact Zimbabwean government cabinet records (99% state records per the 2010 investigation) at Rhodes University as 'personal' papers; repatriated 2012. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Rhodesia Cabinet Files — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/rhodesia-cabinet-files/]

actors.name: Ernie Wolfe III
actors.role: US dealer/collector of African art (vigango trade, 1980s-90s)
actors.why_flag: ORA states, citing the 1999 provenance study of 294 vigango in North American collections (Mitsanze, Udvardy, Giles), that vigango he 'collected from the field' had been stolen from Mijikenda homesteads before he sold them to American buyers. Phrasing restates ORA's published findings, not a legal determination. Modern US-market case — near-zero relevance to BM historic records but retained for pan-African completeness. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Offer to Return 27 Vigango — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/offer-to-return-27-vigango/]

actors.name: Jean-Pierre Daugas
actors.why_flag: ORA documents him as French co-leader of the 1981-84 Rouazi-Skhirat excavations preceding the 1984 transfer of Neolithic remains to Bordeaux — a 'temporary study loan' that became indefinite retention until 2019. Review signal, not an allegation. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Bones of Returned Memory — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/bones-of-returned-memory-the-repatriation-of-neolithic-skeletons-from-bordeaux-to-rabat/]

actors.name: André Debénath
actors.role: Director, French Prehistoric Mission in Morocco
actors.why_flag: ORA documents that he co-facilitated the 1984 transfer of the Rouazi-Skhirat human remains to the University of Bordeaux, where retention became indefinite for 35 years. Review signal, not an allegation. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: ORA: Bones of Returned Memory — https://openrestitution.africa/case-study/bones-of-returned-memory-the-repatriation-of-neolithic-skeletons-from-bordeaux-to-rabat/]

actors.name: Kurt Strümpell
actors.why_flag: PAESE documents him as a Schutztruppe officer 1900-1912 'involved in numerous violent military interventions against the local population' who gave ~700 objects to Städtisches Museum Braunschweig 1901-1908; collection classified historically sensitive — any Strümpell provenance warrants acquisition-context review. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: PAESE subproject '(Post)colonial acquisition histories' — https://www.postcolonial-provenance-research.com/en/paese/teilprojekte/translate-to-english-postkoloniale-erwerbsgeschichten-und-objektbedeutungen/]

actors.name: Wilko von Frese
actors.why_flag: PAESE: 167 Grassfields objects at Landesmuseum Hannover from this officer stationed in Dschang 1908-1910; project states acquisition types include 'appropriations on punitive expeditions' to be examined case by case. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: PAESE subproject 'Conditions of acquisitions in colonial Cameroon' — https://www.postcolonial-provenance-research.com/en/paese/teilprojekte/conditions-of-acquisitions-in-colonial-cameroon/]

actors.name: Julius Konietzko
actors.why_flag: PAESE/Provenienzforschung Niedersachsen document a 1930 sale to Hannover carrying a punitive-expedition provenance claim (Bamenda 1911) and Benin-kingdom object tags; Hamburg port dealer whose stock routinely embedded colonial-military acquisition contexts. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: Provenienzforschung Niedersachsen dealer page — https://www.provenienzforschung-niedersachsen.de/handel/julius-konietzko-hamburg/]

actors.name: Wilhelm Langheld
actors.why_flag: PAESE documents the Langheld brothers' German East Africa collections (1889-1901) with an acquisition spectrum explicitly including robbery; officer-collector provenance from this network warrants review. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: PAESE database/subprojects — https://www.postcolonial-provenance-research.com/en/database/]

actors.name: Johannes Langheld
actors.role: Colonial-era collector (Langheld brothers, German East Africa)
actors.why_flag: PAESE-indexed member of the Langheld brothers' 1889-1901 German East Africa collecting network, whose documented acquisition spectrum includes robbery. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: PAESE database — https://www.postcolonial-provenance-research.com/en/database/]

channels.name: Army prize system (prize committees, agents, auctions)
aliases: Army prize system (prize committees, agents, auctions)
channels.type: military prize system (official loot collection and auction)

channels.why_flag: Appointed to sell the Asante indemnity gold; paid £11,000 for hundreds of items and sold them from their Haymarket showrooms in April 1874 (records lost in WWII); the BM bought 12 items directly from Garrard in 1874. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: V&A Asante gold — https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/a-history-of-asante-gold-at-the-vanda ; BM Asante Gold Regalia]

India Office / Secretary of State for India transfers

[suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: BM Maqdala collection — https://www.britishmuseum.org/about-us/british-museum-story/contested-objects-collection/maqdala-collection]

channels.name: Royal gift/trophy channel (Queen Victoria presentations)
channels.why_flag: Six Maqdala manuscripts went to the Royal Library at Windsor; the Khalifa's Black Flag and Zulu royal items seized by Wolseley were sent to Queen Victoria; Wolseley's 1874 Asante gifts were presented at Windsor. 'Presented to the Queen/royal family' after these campaigns is a documented loot pathway. HIGH-VOLUME phrase — calibrate. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: AFROMET; NAM Black Flag; The Witness 2021]

channels.name: Regimental messes and regimental museums
channels.why_flag: Officers bought loot for regimental messes (Colonel Frazer at Dalanta, 1868) and regiments retained trophies (Mahdi's tomb panel at the Museum of the Highlands; dozens of 'taken' Zulu, Niger and Sudan items at the Royal Welsh museum). 'By descent through the regiment' provenance is a systematic review signal. GENERIC — excluded from flat matching; use as KB context. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: AFROMET; Museum of the Highlands; NMS Baggage and Belonging]

Any object or gold with Ancient Ruins Company provenance is a red flag. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: African History Extra; Botswana Gazette — https://www.thegazette.news/features/returning-looted-artefacts-will-finally-restore-heritage-to-the-brilliant-cultures-that-made-them/]

channels.name: J.F.G. Umlauff (Hamburg)
channels.type: natural-history and ethnographica trading house (1868-1974), incl. human remains
channels.why_flag: Leading European dealer that commissioned captains, colonial personnel and travellers to procure ethnographica and human remains via Hamburg's colonial shipping; wholesaled expedition hauls to museums worldwide (incl. 1,827 Frobenius Kasai objects to the AMNH, 1912; Benin objects to MARKK 1900-1937). Umlauff invoices/labels in a provenance chain signal colonial-trade acquisition needing review. Hagenbeck provenance signals show-business/colonial-trade acquisition contexts. Cameroon) across museums — Speyer provenance obscures original acquisition contexts. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: Digital Benin — https://digitalbenin.org/provenance/804 ; Freiburg online collection — https://onlinesammlung.freiburg.de/en/person/Speyer]

Company-agent provenance from the Kasai warrants review. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: RMCA Studies vol. 182 '(RE)MAKING COLLECTIONS' — https://www.africamuseum.be/sites/default/files/media/docs/publications/ENG_Remaking_collections_avec%20cover%20online%20def.pdf]

channels.name: Henri Pareyn (Antwerp dealership; 1928 estate auction)
channels.why_flag: Antwerp's dominant Congo-material dealer from the 1890s, buying on the docks from returning colonial officials and missionaries (acquisition contexts unverifiable); the 1,997-lot 1928 auction dispersed material widely — buyers included Henry Wellcome, 'from whom much came to the BM' (BM's own biography page). Pareyn provenance is a review flag with direct BM relevance. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: BM term: Henri Pareyn — https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/term/BIOG126968 ; ArcGIS StoryMap — https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/f18048fa10294450beda283ae701fd70]

channels.name: Jeanne Walschot (Brussels)
channels.why_flag: Brussels antiquarian trading Congolese material in the colonial era; RMCA notes for her bequeathed Songye statue: 'We do not have any information about the context in which this piece was acquired in Congo' — emblematic of dealer-chain opacity for Belgian-Congo objects. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: AfricaMuseum provenance overview — https://www.africamuseum.be/en/discover/provenance]

channels.name: Colonial expositions (Antwerp 1885; Brussels/Tervuren 1897)
channels.why_flag: Looted objects were showcased at these events (the Ne Kuko nkisi was 'exhibited in Antwerp in 1885'); the RMCA notes the 1897 colonial exhibition seeded the African art trade in Brussels and Antwerp. Exposition provenance often marks conquest-era objects entering Western circulation. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: AfricaMuseum provenance: Nkisi Nkonde; Origin of the collections]

channels.name: Foster's (auctioneers, Pall Mall)
channels.why_flag: Pall Mall auctioneers documented as a source through which Victorian ethnographica collectors (incl. Pitt-Rivers) acquired objects. Early African material with bare Foster's sale provenance dates to the colonial extraction era and lacks field history. NOTE: attribution of specific 1897-99 Benin sales to Foster's was NOT independently verified in this pass. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: Pitt Rivers 'Rethinking Pitt-Rivers': Dealers and Auctioneers — https://web.prm.ox.ac.uk/rpr/index.php/article-index/12-articles/139-dealers-and-auctioneers.html]

channels.name: Christie's (historical African sales)
channels.why_flag: Documented dispersal channel: sold the James Hooper African collection (London, 14 July 1976, among six Hooper sales 1976-82); Christie's Paris 2020 sale drew documented provenance challenges over a Benin plaque and Igbo alusi figures. HIGH-VOLUME GENERIC: excluded from flat matching; a Christie's lot is a mid-chain event to weigh, not a primary flag. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: Christie's 1976 Hooper catalogue; Auction Daily — https://auctiondaily.com/news/benin-bronzes-and-the-auction-world-past-present-and-future/]

channels.name: London Missionary Society museum dispersal (1910)
channels.why_flag: The LMS museum (1814-1910), holding African and Malagasy material incl. converts' surrendered 'idols', was dispersed April-May 1910: first pick to the British Museum (C.H. Read), then Pitt Rivers (Balfour), collector A.W.F. Fuller, dealer W.O. Oldman and the Horniman; remainder auctioned at Stevens' 31 May 1910. 'Ex-LMS' provenance signals missionary-era acquisition contexts requiring review. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: Journal of the History of Collections 29:1 — https://academic.oup.com/jhc/article/29/1/109/2503285]

channels.name: Cranmore Ethnographical Museum dispersal (post-1939)
channels.why_flag: Harry Beasley's 6,000+ object museum (incl. African/Benin material) was distributed after his 1939 death to the BM, Edinburgh, Cambridge, Pitt Rivers and Merseyside museums, with further private sales by his widow (to 1974) and daughters. Cranmore/Beasley accession lines are mid-chain — original colonial acquisition needs tracing. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: BM term Cranmore — https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/term/BIOG122477]

channels.name: Pitt-Rivers second collection (Farnham Museum) dispersal
channels.type: private museum dispersal via dealers and salerooms (1960s-70s)
channels.why_flag: The Pitt-Rivers family's private Farnham collection — rich in colonial-era ethnographica bought 1880-1900 from dealers like Webster — was sold onto the open market through Sotheby's and London dealers (incl. K.J. Hewett) in the 1960s-70s. A 1960s-70s London sale of 'Pitt-Rivers collection' material re-dates but does not clean the Victorian colonial acquisition. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: Rethinking Pitt-Rivers: The Farnham Collection — https://rpr.prm.ox.ac.uk/index.php/objectbiographies/29-uncategorised/2-the-farnham-collection.html]

channels.name: British Empire Exhibition, Wembley (1924-25)
channels.why_flag: Objects shipped from the colonies for display (e.g., the Nigerian Pavilion) were sold or transferred into collections at the exhibition's close — Henry Wellcome bought Nigerian Pavilion material in 1925 (38 objects now at the Fowler); the BM records the exhibition as an acquisition source. 'Wembley 1924' provenance means colonial-administration shipment with makers/owners rarely compensated or consulted. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: Fowler Museum — https://fowler.ucla.edu/exhibitions/on-display-in-walled-city/ ; BM term — https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/term/BIOG121573]

channels.name: Leverhulme executors' sales (1926)
channels.why_flag: After Viscount Leverhulme's death his collections were sold in multi-part 1926 sales (London and New York), returning material — incl. ethnographica from a collector with West African business interests — to the trade. 'From the Leverhulme sale, 1926' is a re-entry point into the market, not an origin. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: Anderson Galleries catalogue (Internet Archive) — https://archive.org/details/gri_33125016632586]

channels.name: Elder Dempster shipping network (to Liverpool Museum)
aliases: Elder Dempster shipping network (to Liverpool Museum)
channels.why_flag: Elder Dempster steamers between Liverpool and West/Central African ports moved thousands of objects to the Liverpool Museum via crew (chiefly Arnold Ridyard) and ~200 shore contacts — traders, colonial officials, missionaries and African intermediaries. Acquisition circumstances vary object-by-object (gift, purchase, surrender, loot: incl. an 1899 Benin bronze) — Elder Dempster provenance triggers case-level review. [suspicion signal for review, not proof; source: Tythacott — https://eprints.soas.ac.uk/18676/ ; NML — https://www.liverpoolmuseums.org.uk/stories/reconnecting-ancestors-world-museum]
